name: Montirelin

lead: Montirelin is a modified version of TRH built to last longer and act more strongly in the brain.
It has been tested in rodents and cell cultures for memory, arousal and neuroprotection. Human evidence is limited to a brief reported study in patients with impaired consciousness.

paras: It binds TRH receptors, raising TSH and prolactin and stimulating cholinergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic activity in animal brains.[3][5][8]

No safety profile in healthy people has been published in the sources reviewed. Animal studies report effects on blood pressure and heart rate, and its endocrine actions mirror TRH.[7] It is not described as an approved drug.

lead: Montirelin (CG-3703, NS-3) is a synthetic analogue of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) designed to be more stable, longer acting and more centrally active than the natural hormone. Wikipedia traces its origins to patents held by the German company Gruenenthal.[1]

Published work describes effects on arousal, memory, neuroprotection and neurotransmitter turnover in laboratory animals and cultured cells.[2][3][4][5] The Wikipedia article reports a human study in patients with neurological disturbances but states no regulatory approval; no source reviewed documents appearance-related use.[1]

paras: Montirelin binds TRH receptors in the brain and, like TRH, can release TSH and prolactin; unlike TRH, it is described as orally usable and longer lasting.[1] Rat studies of NS-3 report that it enhanced brain noradrenaline and dopamine turnover and altered blood pressure, heart rate and catecholamine levels.[6][7] Receptor-binding and pharmacokinetic analyses of TRH analogues, and transport studies in intestinal cell models, have examined how such analogues reach the brain.[8][9][10]

In rats with memory disruption caused by lesions or a noradrenergic neurotoxin, NS-3 reversed passive-avoidance deficits, with the authors attributing this to stimulation of cholinergic and noradrenergic systems.[4] Cell studies found that montirelin and other stable TRH analogues protected cultured neurons from several toxic insults.[3][5] Another study reported that TRH excites histamine neurons involved in arousal, relevant to the interest in TRH-like agents for narcolepsy.[2] Wikipedia lists animal findings in concussion, cerebral ischemia, narcolepsy, seizures and spinal trauma.[1]

Wikipedia reports a human study in which patients with neurological disturbances of consciousness showed improvement in 73% after 14 days of treatment; no details of design beyond that were located, and no randomized controlled trial was found in the sources reviewed.[1] Otherwise: no studies found.
